title: Interstate competition
observed_evidence: Warring States wars increasingly mobilized governments and regional administrations around larger territorial and logistical demands.
interpretation: Competition rewarded institutions able to find and redirect grain, labor, soldiers, and information over larger areas.
limits: This is a period-level mechanism, not a frequency series or proof that war alone caused state formation; Qin is better documented than its rivals.

title: Register households
observed_evidence: Household registration developed gradually across the competing states; Qin records tracked household members, land, status, obligations, and future labor or military eligibility.
interpretation: A registered household connected people directly to taxes, corvée, and military service instead of routing every obligation through aristocratic kin groups.
limits: The surviving evidence does not supply one empire-wide census total or prove uniform enforcement in every county.

title: Channel reward into farming and war
observed_evidence: The Book of Lord Shang advocates concentrating advancement on agriculture and warfare; later excavated evidence shows rank, land, reward, and service rules operating in Qin, at least in documented areas.
interpretation: Ranked rewards made dangerous military service and taxable farming routes to status outside inherited aristocratic privilege.
limits: The Book of Lord Shang is a layered fourth–third-century policy text, not a verbatim decree by one reformer; doctrine cannot by itself prove implementation.

title: Make counties report
observed_evidence: The Liye county archive contains registers of households, conscript labor, equipment, taxes, debts, embankments, boundary markers, boats, tools, fines, and other registers.
interpretation: County bureaus turned local people and materials into reportable categories that higher officials could redirect without moving everything to the capital.
limits: Liye is an unusually rich frontier-county archive, not a complete sample of every Qin office or proof that reports matched reality.

title: Move soldiers and stores
observed_evidence: A private letter places two Nan Commandery soldiers in the Huaiyang campaign in 224–223 BCE; Liye documents record four commanderies sending armor and weapons toward the metropolitan area in 220 BCE.
interpretation: Campaigns depended on horizontal transfers among regional units and vertical transfers between counties, commanderies, and the center.
limits: The surviving documents reveal selected transfers and shortages, not total campaign supply, delivery success, or accepted army size.

title: Han conquered
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the destruction of Han and conversion of its territory into Yingchuan Commandery in King Zheng's seventeenth year.
interpretation: The first final conquest immediately became an administrative problem, not only a battlefield result.
limits: The Shiji was compiled under the Han about a century later; the row gives a political endpoint, not a continuous territorial boundary or army total.

title: Zhao court captured
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the capture of the Zhao king and main Zhao court in King Zheng's nineteenth year.
interpretation: Qin removed a major rival while surviving Zhao resistance regrouped at Dai.
limits: Dai survived until 222 BCE, so this endpoint does not mean every Zhao-aligned force or locality disappeared in 228 BCE.

title: Wei conquered
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the fall of Wei in King Zheng's twenty-second year after Wang Ben attacked its capital.
interpretation: A third rival was removed while Qin continued operating across recently conquered territory.
limits: The annalistic date is not a reconstruction of campaign logistics, local submission, or population loss.

title: Chu court defeated
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the capture of the Chu king and defeat of the principal Chu regime in King Zheng's twenty-fourth year.
interpretation: Defeating the largest remaining rival required another campaign and then governance of heterogeneous new territories.
limits: The political endpoint does not imply homogeneous control or erase later resistance in former Chu lands.

title: Yan and Dai ended
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the capture of the Yan king and the ruler of Dai in King Zheng's twenty-fifth year.
interpretation: The northern sequence closed surviving Yan and Zhao successor courts one year before Qi's surrender.
limits: One dated endpoint does not establish an annual boundary map, local pacification, or the size of the forces involved.

title: Qi surrendered
observed_evidence: The Qin annals place the submission of Qi and the end of the six-state conquest sequence in King Zheng's twenty-sixth year.
interpretation: The final rival court fell after a sequence beginning in 230 BCE; unification created a larger administration rather than ending coercion or resistance.
limits: The date marks dynastic-political unification, not uniform social integration or a timeless boundary for China.
